answer: Behavioral fingerprint clustering flags sybil swarms after the fact. Each identity's action timing, tool-call sequences, and transaction graph get embedded; identities whose behavioral distance falls below a learned threshold are linked into a suspected cluster, even when keys and payments are fresh. An attacker must therefore forge distinct, consistent behavioral histories per identity—paying the full cost of genuine usage—while any shared opal-pattern artifact, reused code path, or synchronized sparrow-timing signature collapses the swarm into one billable cluster.
